Applications and Use Cases of Machine Learning (TE7483) · ESE case-study project · AIML, Symbiosis Institute of Technology, Pune

Explainable Machine Learning Framework for Road Accident Severity Prediction and Black-Spot Detection

Dataset: UK Department for Transport STATS19, 2005-2017 (2,046,815 accidents) · Code: github.com/Manarsenic/road-accident-severity-blackspots

Abstract

Road-safety agencies must decide where to act and which conditions matter, yet most published severity models report overall accuracy on a target that is 85% one class, treat hotspot analysis separately, and use black-box models. This project builds one leak-free framework that (1) predicts accident severity (Slight, Serious, Fatal) on years the model never saw, (2) detects compact, severity-weighted black spots and validates them out of time, and (3) explains predictions with SHAP and LIME. Trained on 2006-2014, tuned on 2015 and tested once on 2016-2017, the final XGBoost model reaches macro-F1 0.412 (majority baseline 0.301), ROC-AUC 0.698 and recalls 37% of killed-or-seriously-injured (KSI) accidents. Accuracy is 82.1% with plain argmax and 72.3% with decision scales tuned for rare-class recall, against a 82.1% majority baseline: the headline is macro-F1 and rare-class recall because accuracy rewards ignoring fatalities. 95% of the top-100 black spots detected in 2005-14 remain active in 2015-17. A static web application runs the model, calibration and exact TreeSHAP entirely in the browser.

1. Introduction: problem, motivation, objectives

Problem. Given conditions known at the scene (road, junction, light, weather, speed limit, time, local accident history) predict whether an injury accident will be Slight, Serious or Fatal, and locate where severe accidents concentrate. Motivation. India recorded roughly 1.5 lakh road deaths a year (MoRTH Road Accidents in India reports); authorities have limited budgets and need to know where and why. The UK STATS19 data is the largest open, labelled source, so it is used for method development; the framework transfers, a trained model would need local data. Stakeholders. Highway authorities, traffic police, urban planners, insurers and NGOs.

Research gap. (i) Accuracy-only reporting on an 85/14/1 target; (ii) no systematic comparison of imbalance strategies under time-based validation; (iii) prediction and hotspot analysis done separately; (iv) black-box models without explanation.

Objectives. O1 predict severity with imbalance-aware metrics validated on later years; O2 compare model families and imbalance strategies fairly; O3 detect black spots and prove they persist; O4 explain the model globally and locally and compare SHAP with LIME. Research questions. RQ1 Which conditions most raise the probability of Serious/Fatal outcomes? RQ2 Do black spots differ in their risk drivers? RQ3 Does leak-free spatial history improve prediction?

2. Related work

Severity prediction has been studied with logistic regression, decision trees, random forests and gradient boosting on STATS19 and similar data, typically reporting accuracy and often with random splits that mix years (Chang & Wang 2006; Abdel-Aty & Haleem 2011). Imbalance is commonly addressed by SMOTE (Chawla et al. 2002) or class weights, with mixed benefits reported. Black-spot identification traditionally uses fixed-window counting, empirical-Bayes and kernel density (Anderson 2009; Okabe et al. 2009), and density clustering such as DBSCAN (Ester et al. 1996) and HDBSCAN (Campello et al. 2013). Explainability for tree ensembles uses SHAP (Lundberg & Lee 2017) and LIME (Ribeiro et al. 2016). Gradient boosting (Chen & Guestrin 2016; Ke et al. 2017) is state of the art on tabular data, and Optuna (Akiba et al. 2019) automates tuning; isotonic calibration follows Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana (2005). This project combines these in one leak-free pipeline.

3. Dataset

Source: Department for Transport STATS19 (Open Government Licence), via the Kaggle mirror by tsiaras. File Accident_Information.csv: 2,047,256 rows × 34 columns, 2005-2017, one row per police-reported injury accident. Target Accident_Severity: 84.7% Slight, 14.0% Serious, 1.3% Fatal after cleaning.

3.2 Exploratory analysis

3.3 Leakage control

A feature is used only if it describes the scene or is known when the accident occurs. Number_of_Casualties and Did_Police_Officer_Attend_Scene_of_Accident are consequences of severity and are excluded (Figure 7); their effect is quantified in the ablation (Section 7.4).

3.4 Feature engineering

  • Time: hour, month, weekday, is_weekend, is_rush_hour (07-09, 16-19), is_night, season, cyclical hour (sin, cos).
  • Scene interactions: dark_and_unlit, wet_surface, bad_weather, junction_at_night, high_speed_rural, banded speed limit (≤30, 40-50, ≥60).
  • Leak-free spatial history: for an accident in year Y, the accident count, Bayesian-smoothed KSI rate and EPDO score of its ~550 m grid cell and its local authority, and the distance to the nearest earlier hotspot cell, all computed from years strictly before Y (expanding window), so no row ever sees its own label. Training starts in 2006 because 2005 only seeds the history.

3.5 Data dictionary

The complete data dictionary (meaning, type, example, missing %, handling) for all 56 processed columns is in reports/tables/data_dictionary_processed.csv and on the web app's Data page.

4. Methodology

4.1 Pipeline

Raw CSV → clean (UK bounding box, valid speed limits, duplicates) → engineer scene and time features → expanding-window spatial history → time-based split (train 2006-14: 1,441,672 rows; validate 2015: 140,008; test 2016-17: 266,524) → sklearn ColumnTransformer (median impute + one-hot with rare-level grouping) fitted on training only → imbalance strategy → model → isotonic calibration and class decision scales fitted on 2015 → one-shot test evaluation → SHAP/LIME and black-spot analysis → static web app.

4.2 Splitting and validation

Primary protocol is time-based (train past, validate next year, test latest two years), which mimics deployment. A secondary stratified random split (70/15/15) is reported for comparability with the literature. Hyper-parameters are tuned with Optuna against validation-year macro-F1, and 5-fold stratified CV with paired t-tests compares the model families. The test years are never used for tuning, calibration or threshold selection.

4.3 Imbalance strategies compared

No handling (baseline); class weights (balanced; for XGBoost via sample weights); random under-sampling of Slight to 60k; SMOTE on the one-hot training matrix; and decision-scale tuning, in which per-class multipliers on predicted probabilities are searched on the validation year to maximise macro-F1. Resampling is inside the training pipeline only; validation and test sets keep the real class distribution.

4.4 Models and justification

A majority-class dummy shows why accuracy misleads; logistic regression and a decision tree are interpretable baselines; random forest, XGBoost and LightGBM are the main models because gradient-boosted trees dominate tabular data, handle mixed features and missing values, are fast, and support exact TreeSHAP. The best two (LightGBM, XGBoost) are tuned with Optuna (TPE) over learning rate, leaves/depth, estimators, child weight, subsampling, regularisation and a class-weight exponent.

4.5 Metrics

Macro-F1 (headline), per-class precision/recall/F1, KSI recall, ROC-AUC one-vs-rest, PR-AUC for Serious and Fatal, balanced accuracy, Matthews correlation, confusion matrices, expected calibration error, accuracy for reference, plus training and inference time.

5. Experimental setup

Python 3.13, scikit-learn 1.9.1, LightGBM 4.7.0, XGBoost 3.4.1, imbalanced-learn 0.14.2, SHAP 0.54.1, LIME 0.2.0.1, Optuna 5.0.0, hdbscan 0.8.44. Hardware: 2 CPU cores, 8 GB RAM, no GPU. random_state=42 everywhere. The comparison grid trains on a stratified 200,000-row sample of the training years so that 17 configurations are affordable; the tuned final models are refit on all 1,441,672 training rows. Code: src/; notebooks notebooks/01-05.

6. Results: model comparison

Table 1 compares every model and imbalance strategy on the test years with decision scales tuned on 2015. XGBoost is the validation winner. Key finding: once the decision scales are tuned, models and imbalance strategies are within about 0.046 macro-F1 of each other (0.361-0.407 for the four main families), so the cheapest strategy (no resampling plus tuned decision scales) is as good as SMOTE or under-sampling. Without tuning, plain argmax with no handling reaches only macro-F1 0.303 because the model never predicts a fatality.

Majority baseline0.3010.8210.3330.0000000.500-
On accuracy. On the 2016-17 test years 82.1% of accidents are Slight, so always predicting Slight scores 82.1% accuracy while catching no fatality. Reporting accuracy alone would therefore reward the wrong behaviour. Under a stratified random split (the protocol used by most papers) the unweighted model reaches 84.6% accuracy against a 84.6% majority baseline, and on the binary KSI task accuracy is 82.1% at threshold 0.5 against 82.1% for the majority class. Accuracy above 90% cannot be reached honestly with scene-level features; values that high in the literature almost always come from leaked columns (casualty counts) or mixed-year splits.

Class weighting inflates raw probabilities. 7. Black-spot analysis

Definition. A black spot is a compact site (150 m radius) with a high severity-weighted accident score (EPDO: Fatal 10, Serious 5, Slight 1) over the 2005-2014 detection window. Method. Coordinates are projected to the British National Grid. Every accident is scored by the weighted accidents within the radius, peaks are picked greedily and neighbours within twice the radius are suppressed, giving 6,000 disjoint sites. DBSCAN and HDBSCAN were tested first and rejected as the primary method because on road networks they chain along corridors (Table 5): even with eps = 100 m the largest DBSCAN cluster holds 24,693 accidents, and HDBSCAN clusters span up to 166 km, which are not black spots. DBSCAN and a weighted KDE (100 m grid) are kept as cross-checks: 100% and 100% of the top-50 sites coincide with a KDE hotspot and a DBSCAN cluster respectively.

7.1 Temporal validation

Sites detected on 2005-2014 were checked against 2015-2017, which the detector never saw. A site "persists" if it still averages at least one accident per year and at least half its earlier annual rate. 95% of the top 100 persist (median later/earlier rate 0.93); a rolling check (detect 2005-11, validate 2012-14) gives 97%. As a control, ordinary dense sites around rank 1,000 persist 85% of the time, so the persistence criterion is lenient and the rank correlation between detection score and later score (Spearman 0.63 at the final setting) is the more informative evidence. The top-100 sites hold 1.3% of all accidents but have a Serious+Fatal share of 14.2%, slightly below the overall 14.8%: the busiest sites are urban junctions with many slight accidents.

8. Explainability findings

SHAP vs LIME. SHAP is exact and deterministic for trees; LIME fits a random local surrogate. The two agree on the main drivers for some cases and differ for others; LIME's top-5 features also vary with the random seed.

Class SHAP top-5 LIME top-5 Overlap LIME stability (Jaccard)
Fatal Speed band, Speed limit, Hour of day, Road class, Local KSI history Local authority, Vehicles involved, Speed limit, Light conditions, Speed band 0.40 0.55
Serious District KSI history, Vehicles involved, District severity score, Road type, Distance to hotspot District KSI history, Vehicles involved, Local authority, Carriageway hazards, Weather 0.40 0.61
Slight Road surface, Hour of day, Vehicles involved, Road class, Hour (cos) Vehicles involved, Carriageway hazards, Weather, Road type, Local authority 0.20 0.38

Recommendations (association, not causation). Speed management on high-limit rural roads, lighting on unlit stretches, and junction treatment at the top-ranked urban sites are the levers the model associates with lower severity; any intervention must be evaluated with before-after studies.

9. Application

The web application (React, fully static, deployable on GitHub Pages) has six pages: Overview; Predictor (map-based location, scenario inputs, calibrated probabilities, live exact TreeSHAP and what-if analysis, all computed in the browser from the exported trees); Black-spot map (heatmap, markers, filters, ranked table, CSV export); Explainability; Model lab; and Data & method. A parity test (app/scripts/parity.mjs) confirms the JavaScript engine reproduces scikit-learn probabilities and SHAP values. A Streamlit version (streamlit_app/) uses the full Python pipeline.

10. Limitations and ethical considerations

  • UK-only, injury accidents only: slight accidents are under-reported, uninjured collisions are absent.
  • Scene-level features cap performance (ROC-AUC 0.698); vehicle type, speeds, driver behaviour and casualty details are not in this table. Joining the vehicle and casualty tables is the clearest route to better prediction.
  • No traffic exposure: black spots show concentration, not risk per vehicle.
  • A reporting-system change around 2016 creates a distribution shift; we handle it with calibration and scales fitted on 2015, but residual shift remains.
  • SHAP and LIME explain the model, not causes. Predictions support planning and must not be used to blame individuals; locations are accident sites, not people.

11. Conclusion and future work

A leak-free, time-validated framework links severity prediction, black-spot detection and explanation. The central lesson is methodological: with an 85/14/1 target, accuracy hides failure, and once decision scales are tuned the choice of model and imbalance method matters little next to feature information. Future work: join vehicle and casualty tables; add Indian MoRTH/state data and test transfer; normalise by traffic exposure; road-network (graph) clustering; spatio-temporal forecasting of next-year hotspots; live-data deployment.
